title: Market Baseline
text:
This market baseline examines Data Engineer-related job postings within the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). The analysis focuses on job volume, salary, location, experience requirements, work arrangement, hiring patterns, and specialized skills.
It uses the 2024 Insurance Carrier dataset from Step 3 (1,908 postings in total). To match the Skill Gap Analysis page, the dataset was filtered to Data Engineer-related roles: Data Engineering, Analytics Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, ETL Engineer, and Data Warehouse Engineer titles. Every number on this page is calculated from that filtered data.
The team identified 29 Data Engineer-related postings from the 2024 Insurance Carrier dataset after applying the project role filter, out of 1,908 postings in total.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Job Volume by Title
The filtered dataset contains 29 postings spread across 10 distinct title variations. The most common title is “data analytics engineer” with 8 postings. Titles are variations of Data Engineer, Analytics Engineer, and Data Engineering Analyst roles.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Salary Distribution









Salary information was available for 13 of the 29 postings. The median annual salary midpoint was approximately $142,230, and the average was approximately $140,990. The salary midpoint ranged from approximately $127,000 to $161,625.
Only 6 distinct salary values appear among those 13 postings, so several postings repeat the same salary range. Because salary information was missing for 16 postings and the remaining sample is small, these results should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Location Patterns









Valid state information was available for 29 of the 29 postings, covering 10 states. Texas, Georgia, Wisconsin, and Arizona each had the most postings, with 4 each, together accounting for about 55% of the filtered postings. At the metropolitan-area level, the largest concentrations (4 postings each) were in Dallas-Fort Worth-Arlington, TX, Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Alpharetta, GA, Milwaukee-Waukesha, WI, and Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler, AZ. The state is the location listed on the posting, which may not be where remote work is actually done.
The state ranking largely reflects office footprint rather than hiring demand by state. State Farm supplies 15 of the postings and lists the same roles at its offices in Arizona, Georgia, Illinois, and Texas, so those states rank high mostly because of one employer. In total, the 29 postings are only 13 distinct jobs (see Limitations).
One Travelers posting is listed in Hartford, Wisconsin. The same title, salary, and 8-year experience requirement also appear in a Travelers posting for Hartford, Connecticut, which suggests the Wisconsin label is a location error in the source data. The posting is counted as listed, so Wisconsin’s count of 4 includes it; it was not reassigned.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Experience Requirements









A minimum experience requirement was stated for 22 of the 29 postings. The typical (median) requirement was 5 years of experience, and requirements ranged from 1 to 8 years. About 55% of the postings that state a requirement (12 of 22) ask for 5 or more years, so these roles lean toward experienced hires. The 7 postings with no stated requirement were kept as missing rather than estimated.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Key Findings and Limitations
The 2024 Insurance sample contained 29 Data Engineer-related postings. Their median annual salary midpoint was approximately $142,230, the most postings were in Texas, Georgia, Wisconsin, and Arizona, the typical minimum experience requirement was 5 years, and 31% of postings stated that the role is remote.
Limitations:

Small salary sample. Salary was listed for only 13 of 29 postings, with 6 distinct salary values, so the salary figures are not representative of the entire Insurance Carrier data-job market.
Duplicate listings. The 29 postings are only 13 distinct jobs, because employers such as State Farm post the same job at several offices. A distinct job here means the same employer, the same title, and the same salary (a missing salary counts as one value). Among the 13 distinct jobs, 8 list a salary, and their median annual salary midpoint is approximately $136,415, compared with $142,230 across all postings. The charts above count every posting.
Few employers. The 29 postings come from 7 employers, and State Farm supplies about 52% of them.
Missing experience and work-arrangement information. Minimum experience was missing for 7 postings and no work arrangement was stated for 20; neither was estimated.
Location is the posting location. Remote roles may be done from anywhere, so state counts show where the posting is listed, not where work must be done.

Skills information was more complete than salary and work-arrangement information. Python (Programming Language), Data Analysis, Amazon Web Services, and SQL (Programming Language) were among the most frequently identified specialized skills in the filtered postings. These findings provide a useful starting point for the project’s Skill Gap Analysis, although the small, employer-concentrated sample limits broader generalization.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
This project focuses on Data Engineering and related career opportunities in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). The goal is to evaluate the career’s opportunities, challenges, and accessibility for entry-level applicants. The evaluation is based on a combination of job market data, skill gap analysis, and industry trends.
Data Engineers design, develop, and maintain the systems and infrastructure needed to collect, store, process, and transform large volumes of data. Their work ensures that organizations have reliable and accessible data for analysis, reporting, and decision-making. As organizations increasingly rely on data-driven operations, Data Engineering has become an important technical career pathway (Snowflake; 365 Data Science).
The insurance industry depends heavily on data to assess risk, develop pricing models, detect fraud, and improve business decisions. Advances in big data analytics and telematics have expanded the information insurers can use to understand customer behavior and evaluate potential risks. As a result, Data Engineering plays an important role in supporting modern insurance operations (365 Data Science; Discover Data Science).
This career evaluation examines salary potential, employment opportunities, experience requirements, and technical skill readiness to assess whether Data Engineering is an attractive and attainable career path for entry-level applicants.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
Career Opportunities
Data Engineering in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241) offers promising earning potential, although job availability and work flexibility present some limitations. The median advertised annual salary midpoint was approximately $142,230, suggesting attractive compensation for qualified professionals. However, this figure should not be considered representative of entry-level salaries. The 29 relevant job postings represented approximately 13 estimated distinct positions across seven employers, indicating that opportunities in the analyzed market were concentrated among a relatively small number of employers.
Work flexibility also remains uncertain. Nine postings explicitly mentioned remote work, while the remaining 20 did not specify a work arrangement. Although remote opportunities exist, the findings do not establish how widely flexible working arrangements are available. Overall, Data Engineering presents attractive earning potential, but applicants should consider the limited observed openings and explore opportunities across different employers and related data roles.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
Career Readiness
While Data Engineering offers promising career opportunities, entering the field can be challenging for students and entry-level job seekers. The median minimum experience requirement was five years among the 22 postings that specified experience, indicating that employers often seek candidates with previous professional experience. These requirements create barriers for beginners and suggest that gaining practical experience through internships, projects, or related entry-level positions may improve career readiness.
Technical skills are another important factor in career preparation. The team’s Skill Gap Analysis identified the largest gaps in Python, Cloud Computing, Git / CI-CD, and Spark / PySpark, highlighting areas that require further development. However, SQL emerged as a relative strength, with an average team proficiency of 3.33 out of 5. This foundation can support further learning in databases, data pipelines, and cloud-based data processing. Overall, strengthening technical skills and gaining hands-on experience would help applicants become better prepared for Data Engineering positions in the insurance industry.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
Conclusion
The findings suggest that Data Engineering is an attractive long-term career pathway in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241), but entering the field can be challenging for entry-level applicants. Competitive advertised salaries make the profession appealing, while experience requirements, technical skill gaps, and the limited number of observed opportunities present barriers for beginners.
Despite these challenges, Data Engineering remains a realistic career goal with the right preparation. Applicants can improve their readiness by strengthening Python, Cloud Computing, Git / CI-CD, and Spark / PySpark, while building on their existing SQL knowledge. Developing practical projects, pursuing internships, and gaining experience in related entry-level positions can help bridge the gap between current qualifications and employer expectations.
Overall, Data Engineering offers promising career potential, but success requires continuous technical development and practical experience.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
This section provides career recommendations for students and entry-level applicants pursuing Data Engineering opportunities in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). The recommendations focus on suitable career pathways, employment locations, potential employers, and technical skill development.
The findings indicate that Data Engineering offers attractive earning potential, but experience requirements and technical skill gaps can make direct entry challenging. Therefore, the recommendations emphasize practical ways to build qualifications, identify relevant opportunities, and prepare for long-term career growth.
The recommendations build on the Career Evaluation, Market Baseline, and Skill Gap Analysis findings.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Career Pathways
Based on the Career Evaluation and Skill Gap Analysis findings, entering Data Engineering directly may be challenging for students and entry-level applicants. The analyzed positions had a median minimum experience requirement of five years, while several important technical skills require further development. Therefore, applicants should consider related entry-level positions that can provide practical experience before transitioning into Data Engineering.
Data Analyst is a recommended starting point for applicants with existing SQL knowledge. This role can help develop experience in querying databases, cleaning data, preparing reports, and working with business information. It provides a foundation for understanding how organizations use data to support decisions.
Junior Data Engineer is a more direct career pathway for applicants who have developed foundational Python, SQL, and ETL skills. Entry-level engineering responsibilities can help build experience with data pipelines, databases, and cloud technologies, preparing candidates for more advanced Data Engineering positions.
Business Intelligence (BI) Analyst is another potential entry-level pathway. This role provides opportunities to strengthen SQL, data modeling, reporting, and data visualization skills while gaining experience working with business stakeholders.
Overall, Data Analyst and BI Analyst positions are practical starting points, while Junior Data Engineer is the most direct pathway toward a long-term Data Engineering career. Applicants should prioritize roles that offer opportunities to develop Python, SQL, cloud computing, and data pipeline skills.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Locations
Location is an important consideration for applicants pursuing Data Engineering careers in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). The Market Baseline identified relevant job postings across 10 states, indicating that opportunities are geographically distributed rather than limited to a single location.
For entry-level applicants, the recommended approach is to prioritize locations with the highest concentration of relevant job postings, while also considering access to internships, related data positions, and professional development opportunities. Areas with multiple potential employers may provide greater flexibility when searching for an initial position or transitioning into Data Engineering.
Remote work should also be considered when evaluating opportunities. Nine of the 29 analyzed postings explicitly mentioned remote work, while 20 did not specify a work arrangement. Applicants should therefore explore remote opportunities but verify each position’s location and work requirements before applying.
Overall, applicants should focus on locations where relevant opportunities are available while remaining flexible about relocation, hybrid arrangements, and related entry-level roles. A broader geographic search may increase access to potential career pathways.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Employers
The Market Baseline identified seven employers advertising Data Engineering and related positions within the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). These findings suggest that applicants should consider both the number of available opportunities and the experience requirements when selecting potential employers.
State Farm is an important employer to consider because it accounted for approximately 52% of the 29 analyzed job postings. This indicates a strong presence in the observed job market, although repeated advertisements do not necessarily represent separate vacancies. Applicants should review State Farm’s opportunities while paying particular attention to required experience, technical skills, and entry-level eligibility.
Rather than focusing exclusively on one employer, applicants should also explore the other insurance companies represented in the dataset. A diversified employer search may provide access to different technologies, work arrangements, and career-development opportunities. Applicants should prioritize organizations offering internships, junior-level positions, or related data roles that provide opportunities to develop practical Data Engineering skills.
Overall, State Farm is a priority employer to investigate based on posting volume, but applicants should compare multiple organizations and focus on positions that align with their current qualifications and long-term career goals.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Skill Development Priorities
The Skill Gap Analysis identified Cloud Computing, Python, Git & CI/CD, and Spark / PySpark as the highest-priority areas for technical development. These skills appeared frequently in the analyzed Data Engineering job postings, while the team’s self-reported proficiency remained relatively low. Addressing these gaps would help improve readiness for Data Engineering careers in the Insurance Carrier industry.
Python and Cloud Computing should be primary development priorities because they are important for building data pipelines, automating processing tasks, and managing cloud-based data infrastructure. Applicants should gain practical experience through programming exercises, cloud training, and projects involving data storage and transformation.
Git & CI/CD and Spark / PySpark should also receive significant attention. Git supports collaboration and version control, while CI/CD practices help automate development workflows. Spark and PySpark provide experience processing larger datasets, making them valuable skills for more advanced Data Engineering responsibilities.
Applicants should also strengthen ETL/ELT and data pipeline development, while building on their existing SQL knowledge. Combining these skills in practical projects can demonstrate the ability to collect, transform, validate, and manage data.
Overall, the recommended approach is to prioritize the largest skill gaps, develop hands-on projects, and build a portfolio demonstrating technical proficiency. This provides a structured path toward stronger qualifications and greater career readiness.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Limitations
The career and skill-development recommendations are based on 29 Data Engineering-related job postings from the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241). Because the sample represents a limited number of employers and positions, the findings may not reflect the entire insurance job market or current hiring conditions.
The Skill Gap Analysis uses self-reported proficiency ratings from three team members on a scale of 1 to 5. These ratings have not been independently validated through technical assessments or professional evaluations. Additionally, the market demand scores are derived from how frequently skills appear in job postings, rather than the proficiency levels employers explicitly require. Therefore, the calculated skill gaps should be interpreted as development indicators, not direct measures of job qualifications.
Insurance Knowledge was included in the team’s self-assessment but excluded from the quantitative Skill Gap Matrix because a comparable market demand score was not available.
The recommended career pathways, locations, and employers are based on the available market evidence and should not be treated as guarantees of employment. Applicants should review current job requirements, verify work arrangements, and consider their individual qualifications when making career decisions.

3. Check the file before loading it
Downloads fail quietly. You can end up with an HTML error page sitting there under a .csv name and not find out until something strange happens three cells later. So nothing gets loaded until it clears four checks:

Is it actually a CSV? Decided by reading the first bytes, not by trusting the file extension.
Is it big enough? Anything under 100 MB is not the real dataset.
How many rows are really in it? This is the one that catches people out. Job descriptions contain line breaks inside the quoted text, so counting lines gives about 13 million against 72,498 real rows. A proper CSV parser is the only way to get the true number.
Are the columns the project needs all there?

multiLine has to be on, same line-break reason as above. Without it Spark splits rows in the middle of job descriptions.

Writes the data out to Parquet. Smaller and faster to read than the CSV, and the same format the Step 2 dataset came in.
The write is skipped when a finished copy is already in place, because parsing 700 MB of CSV is by far the slowest thing in this notebook. The Parquet copy lives in data/Lightcast_JobPostings_2024/ and is gitignored.

def column_group(name):
    """Rough plain-English group for a column, based on its name."""
    rules = [
        (("MODELED_", "LAST_UPDATED", "DUPLICATES", "POSTED", "EXPIRED", "DURATION",
          "SOURCE", "URL", "ACTIVE_", "ID"), "Posting record"),
        (("BODY",), "Job description text"),
        (("TITLE",), "Job title"),
        (("COMPANY",), "Employer"),
        (("EDUCATION", "MIN_EDULEVELS", "MAX_EDULEVELS", "CIP"), "Education"),
        (("EMPLOYMENT_TYPE", "MIN_YEARS", "MAX_YEARS", "IS_INTERNSHIP"), "Job type and experience"),
        (("SALARY", "ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD"), "Pay"),
        (("REMOTE_TYPE",), "Remote work"),
        (("LOCATION", "CITY", "COUNTY", "MSA", "STATE"), "Location"),
        (("NAICS",), "Industry code (NAICS)"),
        (("ONET", "SOC"), "Occupation code (O*NET, SOC)"),
        (("SKILLS", "SPECIALIZED_SKILLS", "COMMON_SKILLS", "SOFTWARE_SKILLS", "CERTIFICATIONS"), "Skills and certifications"),

def parse_posted():
    """POSTED as a real date. Handles the new file's M/d/yyyy and the old file's yyyy-MM-dd."""
    return F.coalesce(
        F.expr("CAST(try_to_timestamp(CAST(POSTED AS STRING), 'M/d/yyyy') AS DATE)"),
        F.expr("CAST(try_to_timestamp(SUBSTR(CAST(POSTED AS STRING), 1, 10), 'yyyy-MM-dd') AS DATE)"),
    )

def profile(df):
    """Counts for one dataset, all in a single pass."""
    title      = F.lower(F.col("TITLE_RAW"))
    in_net     = F.coalesce(title.rlike(NET_REGEX), F.lit(False))
    is_strict  = F.coalesce(title.rlike(STRICT_REGEX), F.lit(False))
    is_ins     = F.col("NAICS_2022_4").cast("string") == "5241"
    one_if     = lambda cond: F.sum(F.when(cond, 1).otherwise(0))
    posted     = parse_posted()
    r = df.agg(
        F.count(F.lit(1)).alias("total_rows"),
        one_if(is_ins).alias("insurance_5241_rows"),
        one_if(is_ins & in_net).alias("insurance_data_role_rows"),
        one_if(is_ins & is_strict).alias("insurance_strict_data_engineer_rows"),
        one_if(is_ins & in_net & is_filled("SALARY_FROM")).alias("data_role_with_salary"),
        one_if(is_ins & in_net & is_filled("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE")).alias("data_role_with_min_years_experience"),
        one_if(is_ins & is_filled("SKILLS_NAME")).alias("insurance_with_skills"),
        F.min(posted).alias("posted_first"),
        F.max(posted).alias("posted_last"),
        one_if(F.col("POSTED").isNotNull() & posted.isNull()).alias("posted_unreadable"),
    ).collect()[0].asDict()
    return {k: (str(v) if k.startswith("posted_") and k != "posted_unreadable" else int(v)) for k, v in r.items()}

# Variance analysis: the Step 2 export against the Step 3 export, file to file.
# Pure Python, no Spark needed, since both are finished CSVs on disk.
from datetime import datetime

STEP2_EXPORT = ROOT / "outputs" / "step2" / "insurance_5241_all_postings.csv"
STEP3_EXPORT = OUT_DIR / "insurance_5241_all_postings_step3.csv"

def parse_posted_text(s):
    """POSTED as a real date. Step 2's file is yyyy-MM-dd, Step 3's is M/d/yyyy."""
    s = (s or "").strip()
    for fmt in ("%m/%d/%Y", "%Y-%m-%d"):
        try:
            return datetime.strptime(s[:10], fmt).date()
        except ValueError:
            pass
    return None

def export_profile(path):
    """Everything we want to compare, in one pass over a finished export."""
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    filled   = lambda c: sum(1 for r in rows if (r.get(c) or "").strip())
    distinct = lambda c: len({(r.get(c) or "").strip() for r in rows if (r.get(c) or "").strip()})
    flagged  = [r for r in rows if r.get("IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH") == "1"]
    dates    = [d for d in (parse_posted_text(r.get("POSTED")) for r in rows) if d]
    return {
        "rows": len(rows),
        "cols": len(rows[0]),
        "flagged": len(flagged),
        "salary": filled("SALARY_FROM"),
        "flagged_salary": sum(1 for r in flagged if (r.get("SALARY_FROM") or "").strip()),
        "minyears": filled("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"),
        "skills": filled("SKILLS_NAME"),
        "companies": distinct("COMPANY_NAME"),
        "states": distinct("STATE_NAME"),
        "first": min(dates).isoformat() if dates else "n/a",
        "last": max(dates).isoformat() if dates else "n/a",
    }

s2, s3 = export_profile(STEP2_EXPORT), export_profile(STEP3_EXPORT)

# (label, key, kind, note). "count" gets a difference and a percent change, "date" does not.
MEASURES = [
    ("Rows in the export", "rows", "count",
     "Every Insurance NAICS 5241 posting in that step."),
    ("Columns", "cols", "count",
     "Identical by design: the same 34 columns in the same order."),
    ("Flagged IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH", "flagged", "count",
     "Same regex in both files, including the ' bi ' term, so these are directly comparable."),
    ("Rows with SALARY_FROM", "salary", "count",
     "Salary present anywhere in the Insurance panel."),
    ("Flagged rows with SALARY_FROM", "flagged_salary", "count",
     "The number that matters: data-role postings we can actually analyse pay for."),
    ("Rows with MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE", "minyears", "count",
     "Empty in Step 2, so experience analysis was impossible on the old data."),
    ("Rows with SKILLS_NAME", "skills", "count",
     "Fully populated in Step 3."),
    ("Distinct COMPANY_NAME", "companies", "count",
     "UNEXPLAINED: Step 3 has more rows but far fewer employers, so the new data is more "
     "concentrated. Check before describing either as 'the market'."),
    ("Distinct STATE_NAME", "states", "count",
     "UNEXPLAINED: 51 is clean (states plus DC), 97 is not a real state count, so Step 2's "
     "field probably holds combined or multi-value entries. Check before mapping it."),
    ("First posting date", "first", "date",
     "Different time window, not just a bigger sample."),
    ("Last posting date", "last", "date",
     "Different time window, not just a bigger sample."),
]

def variance_row(label, key, kind, note):
    a, b = s2[key], s3[key]
    if kind == "date":
        return [label, a, b, "n/a", "n/a", note]
    diff = b - a
    if a == 0:
        change = "n/a (Step 2 is zero)"
    else:
        change = f"{(b - a) / a * 100:+.1f}%"
    share = ""
    if key in ("flagged", "salary", "minyears", "skills"):
        share = f" Share of rows: {a / s2['rows'] * 100:.1f}% to {b / s3['rows'] * 100:.1f}%."
    return [label, a, b, f"{diff:+,}", change, note + share]

variance = [variance_row(*m) for m in MEASURES]

    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["measure", "step2_export", "step3_export", "difference", "percent_change", "note"])

text:
3. Filter to Insurance Carriers (NAICS 5241), flagged for data-role titles
Keep every posting in the Insurance Carriers industry (NAICS code 5241), regardless of job title - nothing gets dropped, this is still the full industry cross-section.
The one addition is a new column, IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH, placed right after TITLE_CLEAN: it’s 1 for postings whose title matches our data-role keyword set (data engineer, data scientist, data analyst / BI, data architect / DBA, data governance, ML engineer, etc), and 0 for everything else.
Sorting or filtering on this column in Excel is how the team can hone in on data roles specifically, without losing the rest of the dataset to work from.


Show code
# This is still the full Insurance Carrier (NAICS 5241) slice - every role, nothing
# filtered out. The only addition is IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH, a 1/0 flag placed right after
# TITLE_CLEAN, using our data-role keyword regex. Rows flagged 1 are the data-role subset.
query = """
SELECT
  -- Core identifiers and posting metadata
  ID, POSTED, EXPIRED, DURATION, URL,
  -- Job title fields (raw text plus Lightcast's cleaned versions)
  TITLE_RAW, TITLE_NAME, TITLE_CLEAN,
  -- Flag: 1 if this title matches the data-role keyword set, 0 otherwise. Does not
  -- drop any rows - just marks which ones are in the data-role scope.
  CASE WHEN lower(TITLE_RAW) RLIKE 'data engineer|analytics engineer|etl|data pipeline|data platform|big data|ml engineer|machine learning engineer|data architect|database|data scientist|data science|data analyst|business intelligence| bi |data governance|data management'
       THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH,
  -- Employer info
  COMPANY_NAME, COMPANY_IS_STAFFING, EMPLOYMENT_TYPE_NAME,
  -- Experience and education requirements
  MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE, MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE, IS_INTERNSHIP,
  MIN_EDULEVELS_NAME, MAX_EDULEVELS_NAME,
  -- Pay
  SALARY, SALARY_FROM, SALARY_TO, ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD,
  -- Location and remote status
  REMOTE_TYPE_NAME, LOCATION, CITY_NAME, STATE_NAME, MSA_NAME,
  -- Industry and occupation codes
  NAICS_2022_4, SOC_2021_4_NAME, ONET_NAME,
  -- Skills and certifications requested in the posting
  SKILLS_NAME, SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME, COMMON_SKILLS_NAME,
  SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME, CERTIFICATIONS_NAME
FROM jobs
WHERE NAICS_2022_4 = '5241'
ORDER BY TITLE_NAME, TITLE_RAW
"""
insurance = spark.sql(query)
insurance.createOrReplaceTempView("insurance_jobs")
print("Insurance Carrier (NAICS 5241) postings:", insurance.count())
print("Rows flagged IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH = 1:", insurance.filter("IS_DATA_ROLE_MATCH = 1").count())

The analysis identified 27 data-related job postings within Insurance Carriers (NAICS 5241). No duplicate job IDs were found.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
This analysis evaluates how well the team’s current skills align with the skills most frequently requested for Data Engineer-related roles in the Insurance industry.
The analysis began with 1,908 Insurance industry job postings. To focus on our target career, the dataset was filtered to Data Engineer and closely related positions, including Data Engineering, Analytics Engineer, Data Platform Engineer, ETL Engineer, and Data Warehouse Engineer roles. This resulted in 29 Data Engineer-related job postings used for the market skill analysis.
The analysis focused on the following Data Engineering skills:
Python, SQL, ETL/Pipelines, Cloud Computing, Spark/PySpark, Databricks, Data Modeling, Databases/Snowflake, Git/CI-CD, and Data Quality/Governance.


Each team member rated their current proficiency using a 1–5 scale:

1 = Beginner
2 = Basic Knowledge
3 = Intermediate
4 = Advanced
5 = Expert

The individual ratings were averaged to calculate the Team Average for each skill.
Market demand was calculated by measuring the percentage of the 29 relevant job postings that mentioned each skill. The percentages were then converted to a 1–5 market-demand scale:

1 = Less than 20% of postings
2 = 20%–39.9%
3 = 40%–59.9%
4 = 60%–79.9%
5 = 80%–100%

The Market Score measures how frequently employers request a skill; it does not represent the proficiency level employers expect.
The skill gap was calculated as:
Skill Gap = Market Score − Team Average
If the Team Average was greater than the Market Score, the gap was recorded as zero.
Development priority was classified as:

High Priority: Skill Gap ≥ 2
Moderate Priority: Skill Gap ≥ 1 and < 2
Low Priority: Skill Gap < 1

A larger gap therefore represents a skill that appears frequently in the analyzed job postings but where the team’s current proficiency is comparatively lower.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Key Findings
The Skill Gap Analysis identified several important areas for technical skill development among the team. Cloud Computing and Python showed the largest measured skill gaps (3.67 each), followed by Git/CI-CD and Spark/PySpark (3.00 each). These skills appeared frequently in the analyzed job postings, while the team’s current proficiency ratings were relatively low, making them the highest priorities for further development.
ETL/Pipelines showed a moderate skill gap of 1.67, with market demand of 62% and a team average proficiency of 2.33. In comparison, SQL was one of the team’s stronger technical skills, with a team average of 3.33 and a relatively small measured gap of 0.67. Data Quality, Data Modeling, DB/Snowflake, and Databricks showed no measured gaps under the current scoring method. However, a zero gap does not necessarily indicate that the team has mastered these skills or meets every employer’s expectations.
Insurance Knowledge was included in the team’s self-assessment but excluded from the quantitative skill-gap comparison because the structured job-posting data did not provide a directly comparable measure of industry-specific knowledge.
The analysis was based on 29 Data Engineer-related job postings in the Insurance Carrier industry (NAICS 5241), published between May and September 2024. Market demand was converted into a 1–5 score based on how frequently each skill appeared in the postings, rather than the proficiency level required by employers. Therefore, the calculated skill gaps should be interpreted as indicators of development priorities rather than direct measurements of employer-required proficiency. These findings reflect the analyzed sample and should not be generalized to the entire insurance industry.
